_what_this_is: The four secure-version-number cases, each appraised under BOTH the live
policy and the frozen one it replaced, and what every cell must produce.
bash rats/test_svn_policy.sh reads this, re-derives all eight cells from
captures already in the repository, and fails when any of them disagrees.
.github/workflows/ci.yml runs it.
Why both policies. Changing an appraisal rule is worth nothing on its own;
what is worth something is being able to show WHICH verdicts moved and
which did not. One column is the rule as DMTF's sample writes it — the
secure version number compared for equality. The other is the rule as this
project writes it — per index, and one-sided. The same four captures and
the same signed reference value go through both.
The four captures are real handshakes, taken on 2026-09-10 with the
responder reading four different measurement fixtures. The evidence is the
528-byte measurement record sliced out of each MEASUREMENTS message, not
the fixture file: appraising the fixture would compare a document against
itself and pass for every input. rats/README.md says the same at length.
★ All four share ONE reference value, rats/ref/clean.corim, minted from the
clean capture. Minting one per case is the mistake that makes every case
pass while looking thorough, because the evidence and the reference would
then come from the same bytes.
_outcome_changes_expected: ★ The assertion the whole file exists for. Exactly one of the four cases
may reach a different VERDICT under the two policies. A change that moved
two cells would have loosened something besides the version rule, and a
change that moved none would not have done anything.

S-eq.proves: the control. The device is exactly what the reference value describes, so anything but a pass in either column means the comparison is broken rather than strict

S-up.proves: ★ the cell that moves. A legitimately UPGRADED device — firmware newer than the published reference value — is refused by equality and accepted by the new rule. This is the entire practical case for the change: under the old rule, publishing a reference value turns every machine that takes the next update red

S-down.proves: ★ rollback protection survived the change. Note the before column: equality refuses this with the SAME check, the SAME category and the SAME index as S-up above — the two rows are byte-identical, which is exactly the complaint. The new rule refuses it under its own name, svn_rollback, so a verdict can now say which of the two directions it saw

S-hash.proves: ★ the integrity rule was not loosened. The version number is correct and ONE BYTE of measurement index 1 was changed on the device before it hashed and signed. Both columns refuse it, by digest_mismatch, and neither column's SVN check fires at all. Without this case the honest question — 'you relaxed a rule, did you relax security?' — has no answer but assertion
